rules.title: The configuration file is `nvs.toml`, and it is TOML
rules.divergesFromPhp: there is no INI dialect: the file is TOML, its name is `nvs.toml`, and no `php.ini` carries over under any syntax because the directive set shares almost no key with it

rules.title: A size or a duration is a quoted string carrying its suffix, a count is an integer, and `false` removes a ceiling
rules.divergesFromPhp: `memory_limit = 128M` becomes `memory = "128M"` — quoted, because the value is typed and the suffix is part of it — and `-1` for no limit becomes `false`

rules.title: A list is a TOML array, a repeated record is an array of tables, and a dotted key is table nesting
rules.divergesFromPhp: no comma-joined or `PATH`-joined strings: a list of roots is `["/a", "/b", "C:\\srv"]`, which is what makes a Windows absolute path spellable at all

rules.title: A duplicate key is an error, and so is an unknown one — per file
rules.divergesFromPhp: `php.ini` silently takes the last of two copies of a key and ignores one it does not recognise; both refuse the boot here, naming the line

rules.title: The block roster is closed, and each block's directives are argued by the rule that adds it
`nvs.toml` is a deployment file, never a project manifest, and it is never found by walking up
rules.divergesFromPhp: there is no `.user.ini` or `.htaccess` discovered beside the code — the file is read from one directory the operator chose, and it holds no source-tree state

rules.title: The root of the tree is every `--config` in order, else `./nvs.toml`, else the shipped defaults
rules.divergesFromPhp: there is no search path, no `PHPRC` and no compiled-in location: a `--config` list, else `./nvs.toml` in exactly the working directory, else the shipped defaults

rules.title: A host with no configuration file runs on the shipped defaults, which are a complete configuration and not an error
rules.divergesFromPhp: a host without a `php.ini` runs on PHP's built-in defaults, which allow nearly everything; the shipped defaults here deny every capability and start in `production`

rules.title: The resolved root is canonicalized once at boot, announced with every file it reached, and re-read from that stored path on reload
`[[include]]` takes a `path` or a `dir`, never both and never neither, and a `dir` is not a glob
rules.divergesFromPhp: PHP's `--with-config-file-scan-dir` reads a directory in an order the build chose; here a `dir` include is every `*.toml` directly inside it, ascending by filename, written in the file itself

rules.title: An include cycle is refused with the chain named, and nesting past eight is refused as depth
The tree is one ordered stream, a later assignment wins, and every override is recorded with both origins
rules.divergesFromPhp: an include may override the file that pulled it in — the base-plus-local shape — but only because the override is reported; nothing is shadowed silently the way a later `php.ini` line shadows an earlier one

rules.title: A value array is replaced wholesale by a later file; `[[table]]` entries accumulate across the tree
A relative path resolves against the directory of the file it is written in; a command-line path against the working directory
rules.divergesFromPhp: a relative path in `php.ini` resolves against whatever the process's working directory happens to be; here it resolves against the file that wrote it, so a config directory survives being copied whole

rules.title: Any file in the tree may set any directive, `System` class included
rules.divergesFromPhp: there is no `PHP_INI_SYSTEM` versus `PHP_INI_PERDIR` split between files: an included file clears the same ownership bar as the root file and may grant a capability, set `[limits.hard]` or add an `[[extension]]`

rules.title: Every file the configuration reads, and its directory, must be owned by the runtime account or root and writable by nobody else
rules.divergesFromPhp: PHP reads `php.ini` and `.user.ini` whatever their owner and mode; a config file or its directory that any other account can write refuses the boot, on Unix by mode and on Windows by effective DACL rights

rules.title: The ownership check runs on `nvs serve` and on reload; `nvs run`, `config check` and `config dump` read without it, and an unchecked file can grant nothing
`optional = true` covers absence and nothing else, and an absent include is checked at the directory that would hold it
A secret directive has a `_file` sibling, exactly one of the pair is set, and the file's whole content is the value
rules.divergesFromPhp: a credential arrives as a file — `password_file = "/run/secrets/db_password"` — with one trailing newline stripped and nothing else trimmed, rather than inline in the file or interpolated from the environment

rules.title: A secret file another account can write refuses the boot; one another account can read only warns
The boot path and `Core\Config::set` parse a value through one implementation
The configuration is one immutable snapshot a request clones at start, and a reload replaces it whole after validating everything
rules.divergesFromPhp: nothing is re-read on the request path — no `.user.ini` scan, no per-directory override — and a reload that fails leaves the old configuration serving rather than half of each

rules.title: `nvs.toml` states defaults, not ceilings, and every directive carries one of three changeability classes
rules.divergesFromPhp: `ini_set` may widen `memory_limit` here too, but only up to a ceiling the file states in its own block, and a `System` directive has no `ini_set` at all

rules.title: A CLI flag that sets a directive is one of a closed list, wins over every file, and there is no `--set`
rules.divergesFromPhp: there is no `php -d key=value`: argv is world-readable and would be a second spelling of the whole format, so only the flags a rule introduces by name reach a directive

rules.title: Reloadability is a second registry field, `Reload` or `Boot`, orthogonal to the changeability class
rules.divergesFromPhp: there is no `PHP_INI_SYSTEM` bundle meaning both "the file only" and "read once at boot"; the two questions are two fields

rules.title: A ceiling is a `System` directive with the default's key name, and `false` removes it
rules.divergesFromPhp: there is no `-1` meaning unlimited; a ceiling is removed with `false` in a root-owned block, and never from a script — and PHP's one `max_execution_time`, CPU time on Linux and elapsed time on Windows, is two keys: `cpu_time` and `wall_time`

rules.title: A directive is `System` when changing it from inside a request would affect something other than that request, and that is all `System` means
Every runtime change lives in the request's own overlay and dies with the request
rules.divergesFromPhp: an `ini_set` never outlives the request even under a long-running process, and no other request can observe it

rules.title: A refused `Core\Config::set` returns `false` and leaves the value unchanged; it is never clamped
rules.divergesFromPhp: `false` is what PHP returns too, but a value above the ceiling is refused whole rather than run at some other number

rules.title: `ini_set` is `Core\Config::set`, and the whole family crosses as strings
rules.divergesFromPhp: `ini_set`, `ini_get`, `ini_restore` and `ini_get_all` are static members of `Core\Config`, a refused set answers `false` and moves nothing, and an accepted one is request-local

rules.title: An edited source file reaches the next request that resolves it, through lazy revalidation and one pointer swap, never a watcher or a restart
rules.divergesFromPhp: `opcache.validate_timestamps` shape, but the cache key is the file's content hash rather than its path, so a stale `mtime` never serves stale code, and there is no `opcache_reset()`

rules.title: A file is resolved once per isolate, so an edit is invisible to a request already running
A revalidated file that no longer compiles fails the requests that resolve it afterwards, loudly, and the last good version is never served in its place
rules.divergesFromPhp: the same behaviour as `validate_timestamps`, chosen over the more forgiving keep-serving policy some caches adopt

rules.title: A reload reports what it applied, names every changed `Boot` key it could not apply, and counts the units it invalidated
rules.divergesFromPhp: a changed listen address is named in the reply rather than silently ignored until the next restart

rules.title: The server is controlled over one local socket whose owner and mode are the authentication, and `nvs ctl` is its client
rules.divergesFromPhp: there is no `SIGUSR2`, no `php-fpm reload` and no signal at all; the operator speaks HTTP to a local socket and gets a report back

rules.title: There is no network-reachable control surface, in either direction of configuration
`nvs ctl config` reports what the running process actually holds, including an optional include that appeared after boot
`nvs config check` and `nvs config dump` resolve the tree with no server, and `dump --origin` names where every value came from
rules.divergesFromPhp: `php --ini` names the files read and `phpinfo()` prints values from inside a request; here one offline command validates the whole tree in CI and names, per key, the file and line that set it and the one it overrode

rules.title: A run mode is one of exactly two closed values, and with nothing configured it is `production`
rules.divergesFromPhp: there is no `php.ini-development`/`php.ini-production` pair to copy and no `APP_ENV`; staging is `production` with different configuration, not a third value

rules.title: The mode a server starts in comes from `nvs.toml` or from `nvs serve --mode=`, and the flag is the last word
No environment variable selects the run mode — not `NVS_MODE`, not `APP_ENV`, not `NODE_ENV`
rules.divergesFromPhp: `APP_ENV` and its kind are ordinary `Core\Env::get` values with no effect on the runtime; the operator's switch is a reload of the root-owned file

rules.title: A mode is a shorthand for the defaults of five `Runtime` directives, and governs nothing else
rules.divergesFromPhp: "what does development mode change?" has a closed, printable answer, which no `APP_ENV` or `NODE_ENV` convention can give

rules.title: A mode also selects three startup defaults that are fixed at boot, never re-derived, and never flippable from code
A program may read the mode and may flip it for its own request, bounded by a `System` ceiling
rules.divergesFromPhp: a script can turn development defaults on for itself only where the operator opened a ceiling, and the flip never reaches another request

rules.title: An application is its entry file path, and an `[[app]]` block is keyed on a `root` directory or one `entry` file
rules.divergesFromPhp: a per-directory `php.ini`, a `.user.ini` or a PHP-FPM pool keys on a directory the web server chose; an `[[app]]` block keys on the entry file's own path, so `nvs run` has the same identity as a served request

rules.title: Both sides of an `[[app]]` match are canonicalized first, and a key naming nothing examinable refuses the boot
`origin` and `mode` sit on the `[[app]]` block itself, and there is no global `[app]` table
Every matching `[[app]]` block applies, least-specific `root` first, and two blocks on one canonical path are a duplicate
rules.divergesFromPhp: PHP applies the nearest `.user.ini` and stops; here a host-wide block and an application's own block compose, the narrower one winning only the keys it states

rules.title: An `[[app]]` block may widen a limit or grant a capability up to the global ceiling, and may only lower its own ceiling
rules.divergesFromPhp: a per-directory `php.ini` can only move what `PHP_INI_PERDIR` allows; an `[[app]]` block sets any `[app.limits]` value up to `[limits.hard]` and grants a capability the global block withholds, so the root file denies and each application states what it needs

rules.title: A `[[server.mount]]` routes and carries no `mode`; an `[[app]]` block sets policy
Scheduled work is a `[[schedule]]` entry firing a `spawn script`, checked at boot, with no runtime API
rules.divergesFromPhp: there is no crontab line and no scheduler API — a job, its cadence and its concurrency policy are an entry in `nvs.toml`, refused at boot when it cannot be armed

rules.title: `cron` is five-field POSIX plus five named shorthands, parsed at boot with the line named
rules.divergesFromPhp: a seconds field or Quartz's `L`/`W`/`#`/`?` is refused at boot rather than accepted by whichever cron the host happens to run

rules.title: `scope` is mandatory with no default, and `fleet` with no shared store refuses to boot
rules.divergesFromPhp: the `flock`-and-hope guard a PHP deployment adds per cron job is one required word per entry, and forgetting it is a boot error rather than four copies of a nightly run

rules.title: Every `[[schedule]]` key is `System`, and not even `RuntimeTighten` reaches one
rules.divergesFromPhp: no `ini_set` or `.user.ini` can add, remove or retime a job — a request cannot touch the schedule at all

rules.title: An entry's `limits` and `grants` narrow the deployment's, and can never widen them
A scheduled run is a root isolate that spends a root's budget, and only `nvs serve` fires one
rules.divergesFromPhp: a cron-invoked `php` process gets no limits, no capability narrowing and no place to report but a mail spool; a scheduled run gets the deployment's `[limits]`, its `[capabilities]` and the escalation ladder because it is an ordinary isolate

rules.title: A `fleet` entry fires once per interval across the deployment under a lease in the shared store — at most once, never exactly once
`overlap` is `skip` by default, `queue` holds exactly one pending run, and `kill` cancels before it starts
A missed fire is never caught up, `timezone` defaults to UTC, and a DST gap or repeat fires exactly once
rules.divergesFromPhp: there is no ambient timezone to fall back on and no anacron-style replay — the interval a host slept through is logged as skipped, not run late

rules.title: A store an operator configured is authorized by the configuring — `cache.shared` is the grant, unscoped, and asks no address
rules.divergesFromPhp: a Redis on loopback needs one grant naming the store, not a host allow-list plus an exception for the loopback range the store lives in

rules.title: A Unix socket is admitted in `[cache.shared] url` and `[db.<name>] host`, and refused from any program-supplied endpoint
rules.divergesFromPhp: `Redis::connect('/run/redis.sock')` and a socket path in a DSN a program builds are refused — the path has to be in root-owned configuration

rules.title: A socket is `unix:` where the key is a URL and a bare absolute path where the key is a host
rules.divergesFromPhp: `redis://`, `rediss://` and `unix:` are the only schemes `[cache.shared] url` reads — a credential is `[cache.shared] password` rather than userinfo, and a database index is `[cache.shared] database` rather than a path on the URL

rules.title: A Unix spelling on a build with no `AF_UNIX` transport is refused at boot, never read as loopback TCP
A program-supplied socket path needs `net.local`, a path-scoped grant carrying no address policy and governing both ends
The extension set is folded into one `env_hash` that both compiled-unit cache keys carry, so an extension change is an ordinary cache miss
`opcache.validate` and its rate cap are `System`, and `validate`'s startup default is chosen by the run mode
rules.divergesFromPhp: `opcache.validate_timestamps` and `revalidate_freq` are `PHP_INI_ALL` in PHP; here no request may touch either

rules.title: The five `opcache.file_cache*` directives are `System`-class, because where compiled code is read from is a code-injection primitive
rules.divergesFromPhp: `opcache.file_cache` and `opcache.file_cache_dir` cannot be moved by `ini_set` or `.user.ini`; only the root-owned file sets them

rules.title: The update-check and telemetry endpoints are compiled-in defaults overridable by `NVS_UPDATE_URL` and `NVS_TELEMETRY_URL`
